# Part 9 draft notes — dark places / debatable readings for reviewer attention

- **«Комонь въ полуночи.» (unit 4)** — the passage's most notorious crux: a bare two-word nominal phrase with no verb at all, isolated by periods on both sides in the 1800 print. No completion is asserted; flagged as possibly elliptical, possibly corrupt (manuscript lost, nothing to check against).
- **«Князю Игорю не быть: кликну стукну земля; въшумѣ трава.» (unit 6)** — a second compressed/elliptical line; rendered via the impersonal dative+infinitive construction ("it is not to be, for Igor, [that he remain held]"), same pattern as the proem's opening line, but the referent of the commotion (Igor's own flight vs. an alarm behind him) is left open.
- **«стругы ростре на кусту» (unit 14, the Stugna line)** — kept the conventional "spread its rills over the thicket" reading (the river in flood overflowing onto bankside scrub) without asserting it as certain; this is a genuinely debated phrase.
- **«Днѣпрь» vs. the Stugna (unit 15)** — flagged that the poem names the Dnepr as closing over Rostislav even though the historical drowning (1093, Primary Chronicle) happened on the Stugna, a Dnepr tributary; noted as possible loose usage or conflation, not corrected.
- **«стугою» / Стугна pun (unit 17)** — flagged the debated wordplay between «стугою» (grief, from туга) and the river-name Стугна just used two units earlier; presented as argued, not settled, per the task's explicit flag.
- **Gzak/Konchak falcon riddle (units 21–25)** — glossed literally: соколъ = escaped Igor, соколичь/сокольца = his son Vladimir Igorevich left captive; Gzak proposes killing the boy, Konchak proposes marrying him to a Polovtsian bride instead, Gzak then objects that this course wins neither prize and exposes them to retaliation ("birds will strike the two of us" — noted as proverb-like and its exact force as debated). Noted (with appropriate hedging) the chronicle fact that Vladimir Igorevich did later marry a daughter of Konchak's, since the poem itself narrates no more than this riddle.
- **Dual number** — flagged carefully and distinctly in two separate places: «претръгоста» (unit 10, 3rd-person dual aorist, "the two of them" = Igor and Ovlur, of their two worn-out horses) vs. «рострѣляевѣ» / «опутаевѣ» / «нама» / «наю» (units 21, 23, 25 — 1st/dat./acc. dual forms, all "the two of us" = Gzak and Konchak). These are two distinct pairs bound by dual grammar and are not conflated in the notes.
- **Spelling inconsistencies kept as printed, not normalized**: Овлуръ (unit 5) / Влуръ (unit 10) for the same helper; дивицею (unit 23, with и) / дѣвицею, дѣвице (unit 25, with ѣ) for "maiden"; аже (units 21, 23) / аще (unit 25) for "if/since" — each flagged in its unit's note rather than silently regularized.
- **Ovlur = chronicle figure identification (unit 5)** — phrased with a hedge ("usually identified by scholars... though names and spellings differ between sources") rather than asserting an exact chronicle name/spelling from memory, since that level of detail could not be verified in this drafting pass.

No modern English translation was consulted; all renderings (including the well-known "Igor sleeps, Igor keeps watch" triad, the Donets dialogue, and the Gzak/Konchak exchange) were built fresh from the 1800 Cyrillic text and ordinary OES grammar.
